L118: Right and left cancellations are also called elementary cancellations. Denote by $\to=\overset{r}{\to}\cup\overset{l}{\to}$ and let $\overset{*}{\to}$ be the reflexive-transitive closure of $\to$ on $F(V_{\Theta})$. Then Lemma cite36†2.2 implies that for $u,v\in F(V_{\Theta})$, if $u\to v$, then $\pi(u)=\pi(v)$. Therefore, if $w\overset{*}{\to}w^{\prime}$ for $w,w^{\prime}\in F(V_{\Theta})$, then $\pi(w)=\pi(w^{\prime})$.
L119: ###### Definition 2.3.
L120: 
L121: A word $w\in F(V_{\Theta})$ is a normal form of $x\in\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}$ if $x=\pi(w)$ and no elementary cancellations may be performed on $w$.
L122: 
L123: Every $x\in\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}$ has at least one normal form, as any word of minimal length in $\pi^{-1}(\{x\})$ must be a normal form of $x$. Denote by $\mathcal{N}$ the set of all normal forms of all elements of $\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}$.
L124: Define the equivalence relation $\sim$ on $F(V_{\Theta})$, which is generated by elementary commutations:
L125: 
L126:  | $$w_{1}x_{i}x_{j}w_{2}\sim w_{1}x_{j}x_{i}w_{2},$$  |
L127: 
L128: for all words $w_{1},w_{2}\in F(V_{\Theta})$, and letters $x_{i},x_{j}\in F(V_{\Theta})$ such that $x_{i}$ and $x_{j}$ are not connected in $\Theta$. The following was proved in (cite20†Aragona and D’Andrea, 2020 , Theorem 1).
L129: ###### Theorem 2.4.
L130: 
L131: The following statements hold.
L132: 
L133:   1. (i)
L134: 
L135: Let $w,w^{\prime}\in F(V_{\Theta})$. If $\pi(w)=\pi(w^{\prime})$ and $u,v\in\mathcal{N}$ satisfy $w\overset{*}{\to}u$ and $w^{\prime}\overset{*}{\to}v$, then $u\sim v$.
L136: 
L137:   2. (ii)
L138: 
L139: Every simplifying sequence
L140: 
L141:  | $$w\to w_{1}\to w_{2}\to\dots\to w_{k}$$  |
L142: 
L143: may be extended to a simplifying sequence ending on a normal form of $\pi(w)$.
L144: ### 2.3 Idempotents in $\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}$
L145: 
L146: For $X\subseteq V_{\Theta}$, denote by $\Theta[X]$ the full subgraph of $\Theta$ with vertex set $X$, that is, $\Theta[X]$ is an oriented graph with vertex set $X$ and for $x_{i},x_{j}\in X$, there is an arrow from $x_{i}$ to $x_{j}$ in $\Theta[X]$ if and only if there is an arrow from $x_{i}$ to $x_{j}$ in $\Theta$.
L147: 
L148: In (cite23†Forsberg, 2017 , Theorem 3.6), the following theorem is proved for a general finite simple oriented graph $\Theta$.
L149: ###### Theorem 2.5.
L150: 
L151: There is a bijection between idempotents in $\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}$ and full subgraphs of $\Theta$ which do not contain any oriented cycles.
L152: 
L153: In the proof, an idempotent is mapped to the full subgraph of $\Theta$ whose vertex set is the content of the idempotent. Therefore, for each $X\subseteq V_{\Theta}$ such that $\Theta[X]$ does not contain any oriented cycles, there exists exactly one idempotent in $\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}$ with content $X$. We denote this idempotent by $e_{X}$.
L154: We denote the following set
L155: 
L156:  | $$\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}=\{X\subseteq V_{\Theta}\mid\Theta[X]\text{ does not contain any oriented cycles}\}.$$  |
L157: ###### Remark 2.6.
L158: 
L159: If $Y\subseteq X\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}$, then $\Theta[Y]$ is a subgraph of $\Theta[X]$, and hence it does not contain any oriented cycles. Therefore, $Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}$.
L160: 
L161: Theorem cite37†2.5 implies the following proposition.
L162: 
L163: ###### Proposition 2.7.
L164: 
L165: The set
L166: 
L167:  | $$\{e_{X}\mid X\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}\}$$  |
L168: 
L169: is the set of all idempotents in $\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}$.
L170: ###### Proposition 2.8.
L171: 
L172: Let $X,Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}$. Then $e_{X}e_{Y}$ is an idempotent in $\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}$ if and only if $X\cup Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}$ and $e_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X\cup Y}$.
L173: ###### Proof.
L174: 
L175: If $X\cup Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}$ and $e_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X\cup Y}$, then $e_{X}e_{Y}$ is an idempotent by Proposition cite38†2.7 . Conversely, if $e_{X}e_{Y}$ is an idempotent, then by Proposition cite38†2.7 , there exists $Z\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}$ such that
L176: 
L177:  | $$e_{X}e_{Y}=e_{Z}.$$  |
L178: 
L179: Taking contents, we get
L180: 
L181:  | $$Z=c(e_{Z})=c(e_{X}e_{Y})=c(e_{X})\cup c(e_{Y})=X\cup Y.$$  |
L182: 
L183: Hence $X\cup Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}$ and $e_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X\cup Y}$. ∎
L184: The idempotent $e_{X}$ can be written explicitly. Note that if $\Theta[X]$ does not contain any oriented cycles, then we can write $X$ as $X=\{x_{i_{1}},x_{i_{2}},\dots,x_{i_{k}}\}$ such that $x_{i_{j}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{j^{\prime}}}$ implies $j<j^{\prime}$ for all $j,j^{\prime}\in\{1,2,\dots,k\}$.
L185: ###### Lemma 2.9.
L186: 
L187: Let $X\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}$. Then for any ordering of the set $X=\{x_{i_{1}},x_{i_{2}},\dots,x_{i_{k}}\}$ such that $x_{i_{j}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{j^{\prime}}}$ implies $j<j^{\prime}$ for all $j,j^{\prime}\in\{1,2,\dots,k\}$, we have
L188: 
L189:  | $$e_{X}=x_{i_{1}}x_{i_{2}}\dots x_{i_{k}}.$$  |
L190: 
L191: Moreover, we have $e_{X}z=ze_{X}=e_{X}$ for any $z\in\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}$ with $c(z)\subseteq X$.
L192: ###### Proof.
L193: 
L194: Denote by
L195: 
L196:  | $$y=x_{i_{1}}x_{i_{2}}\dots x_{i_{k}}.$$  |
L197: 
L198: If $x_{i_{j}}\in X$, then
L199: 
L200:  | $$x_{i_{j+1}}x_{i_{j+2}}\dots x_{i_{k}}$$  |
L201: 
L202: is obtained by multiplying letters that do not admit arrows to $x_{i_{j}}$. Lemma cite36†2.2 implies
L203: 
L204:  | $$yx_{i_{j}}=x_{i_{1}}\dots x_{i_{j-1}}(x_{i_{j}}x_{i_{j+1}}\dots x_{i_{k}}x_{i_{j}})=x_{i_{1}}\dots x_{i_{j-1}}(x_{i_{j}}x_{i_{j+1}}\dots x_{i_{k}})=y.$$  |
L205: 
L206: By induction, we get
L207: 
L208:  | $$yx_{l_{1}}x_{l_{2}}\dots x_{l_{m}}=y,$$  |
L209: for any $x_{l_{1}},x_{l_{2}},\dots,x_{l_{m}}\in X$. This proves $yz=y$ for any $z\in\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}$ with $c(z)\subseteq X$.
L210: 
L211: For any $x_{i_{j}}\in X$,
L212: 
L213:  | $$x_{i_{1}}x_{i_{2}}\dots x_{i_{j-1}}$$  |
L214: 
L215: is obtained by multiplying letters that do not admit arrows from $x_{i_{j}}$. Lemma cite36†2.2 implies
L216: 
L217:  | $$x_{i_{j}}y=(x_{i_{j}}x_{i_{1}}\dots x_{i_{j-1}}x_{i_{j}})x_{i_{j+1}}\dots x_{i_{k}}=(x_{i_{1}}\dots x_{i_{j-1}}x_{i_{j}})x_{i_{j+1}}\dots x_{i_{k}}=y.$$  |
L218: 
L219: By induction, we again obtain
L220:  | $$x_{l_{1}}x_{l_{2}}\dots x_{l_{m}}y=y,$$  |
L221: 
L222: for any $x_{l_{1}},x_{l_{2}},\dots,x_{l_{m}}\in X$, which proves $zy=y$ for any $z\in\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}$ with $c(z)\subseteq X$. Since $c(y)=X$, we have
L223: 
L224:  | $$y^{2}=yy=y.$$  |
L225: 
L226: Hence $y$ is an idempotent in $\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}$. Since $c(y)=X$, it follows that $y=e_{X}$. ∎
L227: ###### Definition 2.10.
L228: 
L229: A word $w\in F(V_{\Theta})$ is said to have no arrows from right to left if
L230: 
L231:  | $$w=x_{i_{1}}x_{i_{2}}\dots x_{i_{k}},$$  |
L232: 
L233: where $x_{i_{1}},x_{i_{2}},\dots,x_{i_{k}}\in F(V_{\Theta})$ are letters, and if there is an arrow from $x_{i_{j}}$ to $x_{i_{j^{\prime}}}$ then $j<j^{\prime}$ for all $j,j^{\prime}\in\{1,2,\dots,k\}$.
L234: Moreover, for $X\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}$, $w$ is said to be $X$-topological if $w$ has no arrows from right to left, $c(w)=X$, and $\ell(w)=|X|$. In other words, $w$ is $X$-topological if there are no arrows from right to left and each letter $x_{i}$ with $x_{i}\in X$ occurs in $w$ exactly once.
L235: ###### Remark 2.11.
L236: 
L237: If $X\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}$, then $\Theta[X]$ is an acyclic oriented graph and hence there exists an $X$-topological word. Also observe that the empty word is $\emptyset$-topological.
L238: 
L239: ###### Lemma 2.12.
L240: 
L241: For $X\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}$, a word $w\in F(V_{\Theta})$ is $X$-topological if and only if $w$ is a normal form of $e_{X}$.
L242: ###### Proof.
L243: 
L244: If $w$ is $X$-topological, then $\pi(w)=e_{X}$ by Lemma cite39†2.9 . Moreover, since no letter in $w$ occurs more than once, no further elementary cancellations may be performed on $w$, and hence $w$ is a normal form of $e_{X}$.
L245: Now assume $w$ is a normal form of $e_{X}$. Since $X\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}$, there exists an $X$-topological word $v$ by Remark cite40†2.11 . Hence, there are no arrows from right to left in $v$, $c(v)=X$, and $\ell(v)=|X|$. By the previous paragraph, $v$ is a normal form of $e_{X}$. By Theorem cite41†2.4 (cite42†i ), we have $w\sim v$. Since elementary commutations only interchange letters that are not connected, the relative order of any two letters that are connected by an arrow is preserved under $\sim$.
L246: Hence, since $v$ has no arrows from right to left, the same is true for $w$. Since $\sim$ also preserves content and length, we have $c(w)=c(v)=X$ and $\ell(w)=\ell(v)=|X|$. This implies that $w$ is $X$-topological. ∎
L247: ###### Lemma 2.13.
L248: 
L249: Let $X,Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}$. If there are no arrows starting in $Y$ and ending in $X$ and $X\cap Y=\emptyset$, then $X\cup Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}$ and
L250: 
L251:  | $$e_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X\cup Y}.$$  |
L252: ###### Proof.
L253: Since $X\cap Y=\emptyset$ and there are no arrows starting in $Y$ and ending in $X$, any oriented cycle in $\Theta[X\cup Y]$ must entirely lie in either $X$ or $Y$. Since $X,Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}$, it follows that there are no oriented cycles in $\Theta[X\cup Y]$, and hence $X\cup Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}$. Let $w_{X}$ be a normal form of $e_{X}$ and let $w_{Y}$ be a normal form of $e_{Y}$. Lemma cite43†2.12 implies that $w_{X}$ is $X$-topological and $w_{Y}$ is $Y$-topological.
L254: Since there are no arrows from right to left in $w_{X}$ and $w_{Y}$, respectively, and there are no arrows starting in $Y$ and ending in $X$, there are no arrows from right to left in the word $w_{X}w_{Y}$. Moreover, we have
L255:  | $$c(w_{X}w_{Y})=c(w_{X})\cup c(w_{Y})=X\cup Y,$$  |
L256: 
L257: and
L258: 
L259:  | $$\ell(w_{X}w_{Y})=\ell(w_{X})+\ell(w_{Y})=|X|+|Y|=|X\cup Y|.$$  |
L260: 
L261: Hence $w_{X}w_{Y}$ is $X\cup Y$-topological. Therefore, Lemma cite43†2.12 implies that $w_{X}w_{Y}$ is a normal form of $e_{X\cup Y}$, and hence
L262: 
L263:  | $$e_{X}e_{Y}=\pi(w_{X})\pi(w_{Y})=\pi(w_{X}w_{Y})=e_{X\cup Y}.$$  |
L264: 
L265: ∎
L266: ## 3 Properties of Idempotents in $\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}$
L267: 
L268: In this section, we give some additional properties of idempotents in $\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}$, which are used in Section cite12†4 .
L269: ###### Definition 3.1.
L270: 
L271: For $X,Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}$, define the predicate $p_{\Theta}$ as follows. Condition $p_{\Theta}(X,Y)$ holds if and only if there do not exist $x_{b}\in Y\setminus X$, $x_{a}\in X\setminus Y$, $r\in\mathbb{N}_{0}$, and $x_{i_{1}},\dots,x_{i_{r}}\in X\cap Y$ such that
L272: 
L273:  | $$x_{b}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{1}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}\dots\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{r}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{a}.$$  |
L274: ###### Remark 3.2.
L275: 
L276: If $r=0$, a chain $x_{b}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{1}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}\dots\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{r}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{a}$ is interpreted as $x_{b}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{a}$.
L277: 
L278: ###### Lemma 3.3.
L279: 
L280: Let $X,Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}$. Then $p_{\Theta}(X,Y)$ holds if and only if there does not exist a directed path in $\Theta[X\cup Y]$ whose startpoint lies in $Y\setminus X$ and whose endpoint lies in $X\setminus Y$.
L281: ###### Proof.
L282: 
L283: If there is no directed path in $\Theta[X\cup Y]$ which starts in some vertex of $Y\setminus X$ and ends in some vertex of $X\setminus Y$, then $p_{\Theta}(X,Y)$ must hold. Assume $p_{\Theta}(X,Y)$ holds. Suppose there exists a directed path
L284: 
L285:  | $$x_{i_{1}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{2}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}\dots\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{k}},$$  |
L286: 
L287: such that $x_{i_{1}}\in Y\setminus X$, $x_{i_{k}}\in X\setminus Y$, and $x_{i_{1}},x_{i_{2}},\dots,x_{i_{k}}\in X\cup Y$. Let
L288:  | $$j_{1}=\max\{j\in\{1,\dots,k\}\mid x_{i_{j}}\in Y\setminus X\}\quad\text{and}\quad j_{2}=\min\{j\in\{j_{1}+1,\dots,k\}\mid x_{i_{j}}\in X\setminus Y\}.$$  |
L289: 
L290: Since $x_{i_{k}}\in X\setminus Y$ and $j_{1}<k$, the index $j_{2}$ is well-defined, and $j_{1}<j_{2}$. Then the directed path
L291: 
L292:  | $$x_{i_{j_{1}}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{j_{1}+1}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}\dots\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{j_{2}-1}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{j_{2}}}$$  |
L293: starts in $Y\setminus X$ and ends in $X\setminus Y$. Moreover, the vertices $x_{i_{j_{1}+1}},\dots,x_{i_{j_{2}-1}}$ lie in $X\cap Y$; by the maximality of $j_{1}$, none of them lies in $Y\setminus X$, and by the minimality of $j_{2}$, none of them lies in $X\setminus Y$. Since all vertices of the directed path lie in $X\cup Y$, the vertices $x_{i_{j_{1}+1}},\dots,x_{i_{j_{2}-1}}$ must lie in $X\cap Y$. This contradicts the fact that $p_{\Theta}(X,Y)$ holds and concludes the proof. ∎
L294: Let $w=x_{i_{1}}x_{i_{2}}\dots x_{i_{k}}\in F(V_{\Theta})$ be a word, where $x_{i_{1}},x_{i_{2}},\dots,x_{i_{k}}\in F(V_{\Theta})$ are letters. A word of the form $u=x_{i_{j_{1}}}x_{i_{j_{2}}}\dots x_{i_{j_{l}}}$ with $1\leq j_{1}<j_{2}<\dots<j_{l}\leq k$ is called a quasi-subword of $w$. Moreover, the empty word is a quasi-subword of any word. From the definition of $\to$, it follows that if $u\overset{*}{\to}v$, then $v$ is a quasi-subword of $u$.
L295: ###### Proposition 3.4.
L296: 
L297: Let $X,Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}$. If $e_{X}e_{Y}$ is an idempotent in $\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}$, then $p_{\Theta}(X,Y)$ holds.
L298: ###### Proof.
L299: 
L300: Assume $p_{\Theta}(X,Y)$ does not hold. We show that $e_{X}e_{Y}$ is not an idempotent. Suppose that, on the contrary, $e_{X}e_{Y}$ is an idempotent. We now construct a contradiction. Let $w_{X}$ be a normal form of $e_{X}$ and let $w_{Y}$ be a normal form of $e_{Y}$. Lemma cite43†2.12 implies that $w_{X}$ is $X$-topological and $w_{Y}$ is $Y$-topological. We also have $\pi(w_{X}w_{Y})=e_{X}e_{Y}$. Since $e_{X}e_{Y}$ is an idempotent, by Proposition cite44†2.8 , we have
L301:  | $$X\cup Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}\quad\text{and}\quad e_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X\cup Y}.$$  |
L302: 
L303: Let $u\in F(V_{\Theta})$ be a normal form of $e_{X\cup Y}$ with $w_{X}w_{Y}\overset{*}{\to}u$. Such a word $u$ exists by Theorem cite41†2.4 (cite45†ii ) and $\pi(w_{X}w_{Y})=e_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X\cup Y}$. By Lemma cite43†2.12 , $u$ is $X\cup Y$-topological.

L15: cite7†View PDF cite8†HTML (experimental) L16: > Abstract:Let $\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}$ denote the Hecke-Kiselman monoid associated to a finite simple oriented graph $\Theta$. We reduce the problem of describing the endomorphism monoid $\mathrm{End}(\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta})$ to determining when a product of two idempotents in $\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}$ is again an idempotent. This yields a procedure for constructing a Boolean matrix monoid isomorphic to $\mathrm{End}(\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta})$.
L17: As an application, we obtain an explicit description of the endomorphism monoid of the Catalan monoid $\mathcal{C}_{n+1}$.
